_comment: What a sector makes, consumes and throws off.
WHY MATERIALS ARE A NODE KIND. The layer could already say that a technology addresses
a constraint and that a project deploys the technology. It could not say what any of it
is made of. That gap is not academic: the prices that decide whether a route pays —
the allowance price, scrap, hydrogen, electricity — are prices OF MATERIALS, and with
nowhere to hang them they were sitting on measures and technologies as if they belonged
to the instrument rather than to the thing being bought. Materials are also the only
object that joins two sectors honestly: blast-furnace slag leaving steel and arriving in
cement is one node with an edge on each side, not a sentence on two pages.
THE FIVE TYPES. `by_product` and `waste_stream` are kept apart deliberately — a
by-product has a buyer, a waste stream has to be paid to take away — because a page that
grouped them would assert a market that may not exist. Captured CO2 is a waste stream
today and would move to by_product the day somebody is reliably paid for it.
EDGES LIVE ON THE MATERIAL. Every edge incident to a material is recorded here, the same
arrangement bottlenecks.json uses, so there is one file to read and one place to gate:
produced_by    sector: | project:   -> this material comes out of it
consumed_by    sector: | technology: -> this material goes into it
substitutes    another material id   -> this one can stand in for that one
required_by    technology:           -> the technology cannot run without it, and does
not consume it (an energy carrier, a catalyst).
Empty on cement: everything here is consumed.
Each edge carries `since` and `evidence`, as every edge in this repository does, and
`volume` where a sourced parameter states one. `volume` names a parameter id rather than
restating a number, so a material cannot carry a figure that is not in parameters.json
with the sentence it was read from.
WHAT IS MISSING. Slag and fly ash — the clinker substitute the brief asks for third —
are not here, and the reason is the rule rather than the effort: no source stating the
substitution has been read, and an edge without evidence is the one thing this layer
does not ship. See GAPS.md, which names the document that would fill it.
crma_annex_i  WHETHER THE MATERIAL IS A STRATEGIC RAW MATERIAL under Annex I of
the Critical Raw Materials Act, brief 5 §2. Null where it is not,
which is both materials on the platform today: clinker and a
captured CO2 stream are neither of them raw materials the Union
has listed. Where it is, the value is the Annex I entry as the
annex words it plus the source it was read from, and the sector
page renders it as a tag on the material — a fact about the
material, never a judgement about the sector that handles it.
The field is REQUIRED and explicit rather than absent-means-no:
an unlisted material and a material nobody has checked are the
same object otherwise, which is the mistake the scope attribute
in ROADMAP.md is written about.

materials.name: Clinker
materials.description: The calcined intermediate that carries almost all of cement's process CO2. A tonne of cement is a tonne of clinker plus additions, which is why every carbon instrument that reaches this sector is written per tonne of clinker rather than per tonne of the product sold.

produced_by.volume_note: EU clinker output is unsourced and is the gap blocking every sector total on this page — see GAPS.md, 'EU clinker output'.

evidence.note: The ETS free-allocation benchmark is set per tonne of grey cement clinker produced, which is the Commission stating what this sector's benchmarked output is.

materials.name: Captured CO2
materials.description: What a capture plant produces and cannot sell. It is abated only once it is stored, so every tonne recorded here is a tonne owed to a transport and storage chain built by other parties on other timetables.

evidence.quote: Brevik CCS will capture around 400,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year, representing 50% of the plant's emissions.

Member States shall take the necessary measures to enable access to CO2 transport networks and to storage sites for the purposes of geological storage of the produced and captured CO2 as far as it is economically feasible to do so or when a potential customer is willing to pay, in accordance with Article 21 of Directive 2009/31/EC.
